title: A review of Mimi Sheraton's book, 1,000 Foods To Eat Before you Die

paragraphs.text: Most people know Mimi Sheraton as the former, highly regarded New York Times restaurant critic. And now, with the publication of her latest book 1,000 Foods to Eat Before You Die, your list of foods to try is about to get a lot longer. Inspired by Patricia Schultz's best-selling book, 1,000 Places to See Before You Die, Sheraton has collected a list of 1,000 must-try dishes, restaurants, markets, cultural feasts, and some foods common to many countries around the world. Sheraton has cleverly put all of them together in one large book, along with detailed and insightful information on historic and cultural context, where to try a particular dish, and even several dozen recipes she has acquired. It's a project that's been 10 years in the making – one that's a wonderful display of Sheraton's vast food knowledge.

Fitting the world's incredible dishes into a mere 1,000 entries, however, is no easy task. 'I actually started with about 1,800 entries that I had to weed down,' says Sheraton, who now says that this was for the best. 'All the while, other foods and dishes continued presenting themselves.' One of her main goals was showing an equal respect for the dishes of say, Australia, as she did for a culinary powerhouse like China. 'Between the United States, France and Italy I could have easily filled the book,' she says, 'but I wanted to give an overall representation of what the world eats. There are interesting things to try... in all parts of the world, so chicken pot pie and strawberry shortcake fell by the wayside to make room for something like East Africa's Zanzibar duck,' a braised, clove-scented duck seasoned with lemon.

So what can we say about the authenticity of the recipes? Having nearly the same number of pages as it has entries, 1,000 Foods highlights everything from Chinese hoisin sauce to the oysters of Locmariaquer, France. I have consulted food critics and chefs from many parts of the word on this matter, and they universally agree that the recipes in the book genuinely reflect the culinary traditions and practice of the countries they come from. However, if I have one reservation, it would be that the visuals that accompany many of the recipes are not at the standard we've become accustomed to in the contemporary cook book genre.

Sheraton organised 1,000 Foods according to the geography of flavour and culinary style rather than strict geographical borders. For the most part, traditional dishes that may be popular internationally are still listed according to their region of origin. For example, a food such as pizza, despite being an American staple, still falls under 'Italy'. This can be a bit confusing at first, but once you get the hang of it, it becomes easy to navigate and has actually proved effective in other books about cooking. Sheraton has also included a special index providing easy links to items such as holiday food, world-class markets, recommended restaurants and recipes. 'Everything in the book has to be available to readers somehow,' she says, 'whether you go to a restaurant, or buy it at a store or online, or even make it yourself, everything here is triable.' The drawback with this kind of approach is that the food scene is never static, and good restaurants can quickly go out of business, so readers may want to double check details online.

In summary, what is the underlying message of this book? Since the link between food and exploration has been evident for centuries, 1,000 foods is as much an investigation of the world and its people as it is a culinary journey. That's because there is a very strong link between food and exploring the far reaches of the planet. 'For me, food helps define a place,' says Sheraton, who says that each place in the world is individual because its cooking styles and dishes are not found anywhere else, that no two culinary traditions are alike. This doesn't just apply to the taste. Sheraton adds that she wants to experience the way a dish is served and how it appears on the plate, whether it is simplistic and casual or much more elaborate. She then goes on to make a comment that I find terrifically interesting, 'I really think that in a world that's becoming more homogenous, if you can find traditional foods in their country of origin... it's as important as looking at a cathedral, a palace or ancient statues'. Furthermore, in an increasingly globalised world where populations are migrating to distant countries, Sheraton says that food can become a daily part of life in a new country, and help migrants keep their heritage alive.

Despite its title, Sheraton's book is much more than a food lover's life list. 'There are so many ways to use 1,000 Foods,' she says, 'whether you're planning to visit a place and want to look up dishes to try while there, or you start from the entry and then travel to the place it suggests.' As a writer, I hope that most people will simply find it to be a good read; dip in and out and maybe strike up an interest that will lead them, their friends and relatives, even further into a certain cuisine or country or customs. Certainly, for those needing that little bit of motivation to get out and experience the sights and tastes of the world, this book is well worth its rather expensive price tag.
